scenes.narration: Design Secure Architectures is the highest-weighted domain on the associate exam, at thirty percent — heavier than any other domain on either exam. And almost every question inside it boils down to one skill: look at a stack of policies and predict, exactly, whether a request gets allowed. This chapter builds that skill from scratch — users, groups, and roles, identity policies versus resource policies, the real order AWS evaluates them in, and S T S, or S-T-S, the mechanism that hands out temporary, cross-account access without a single long-lived secret changing hands.

facts.label: Design Secure Architectures — SAA-C03
facts.value: 30% of the exam — the single highest-weighted domain

facts.label: The load-bearing rule of this chapter
facts.value: explicit Deny → explicit Allow → implicit Deny, every request

scenes.narration: Faced with 'an application needs to talk to AWS,' the instinct that feels fastest is this: create one IAM user per app, hand it a permanent access key, and attach administrator access so nothing ever throws a permission error. Drop that key into a config file or bake it into a machine image, and you're done. For a human doing something urgent, the shortcut is even simpler — just sign in as the root user, since root can obviously do anything. None of this looks careless in the moment. It works on the first try. That's exactly why it's the wrong answer the exam loves to dangle.

props.heading: “One user, one key, AdministratorAccess, done”
bullets: Create one IAM user per application, hand it a long-lived access key pair
Attach AdministratorAccess "to avoid permission errors later"
Bake the key into a config file, an environment variable, or an AMI
For urgent human work, just sign in as the root user instead

scenes.narration: Here's the mechanism behind why each shortcut is worse than it looks. A long-lived access key has no expiry and no automatic rotation, so it sits exactly where secrets leak from — a git history, a plaintext config, a shared machine image — and stays valid until a human notices. Pairing that with administrator access means the least-privilege violation compounds the exposure: whichever leak happens first is now a full account compromise, not a contained one. Root is worse still, because no IAM policy can ever restrict it after the fact. And even correctly-issued role credentials aren't automatically safe — the older, unauthenticated version of the instance metadata service could be tricked into handing over a role's credentials through a server-side request forgery attack, which is why AWS has pushed newer instances toward a session-based, token-gated version by default.

props.heading: A standing liability, not a one-time risk
bullets: Long-lived keys have no built-in expiry or rotation — once leaked, valid until someone notices
AdministratorAccess turns any single leak into a full account compromise
Root can't be scoped by any IAM policy — there's no restricting it after the fact
IMDSv1 was vulnerable to credential theft via SSRF; IMDSv2 closes that with a session token

scenes.narration: Every single API call, no matter which identity made it, gets evaluated the same three-step way. Step one: if any applicable policy — identity-based or resource-based, doesn't matter — contains an explicit Deny, the request is denied, full stop, no matter how many Allows exist elsewhere. Step two: if no Deny was found, but at least one applicable policy contains an explicit Allow, the request is allowed. Step three: if neither shows up, AWS's default posture is implicit deny — nothing is granted by default. This three-step order is the single most tested fact in this entire chapter.

props.heading: How AWS turns a stack of policies into one decision

cells: DENY — wins outright, regardless of any Allow elsewhere

scenes.narration: Here's that rule made concrete, inside an actual policy document. The first statement grants read access to the entire reports bucket. The second is an explicit Deny, scoped to just the confidential prefix inside that same bucket. Walk it through the three steps: for anything under confidential, the Deny applies and wins outright. For everything else in the bucket, no Deny applies, so the Allow stands. Reading a document like this and predicting the outcome instantly is arguably the single most common question shape in the secure-architectures domain.

props.kicker: SEEN IN A REAL POLICY DOCUMENT
props.heading: A broad Allow, narrowed by an explicit Deny
lines: // grants read access to the whole bucket
// this explicit Deny wins here, no matter what the Allow says

scenes.narration: There's a fixed order of questions that gets you to the right identity design almost every time. Start by asking whether the principal in the scenario is a human who needs to sign in, or a workload — an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, an ECS or EKS task — that calls AWS APIs on its own. For humans, centralize through IAM Identity Center, or at minimum groups plus multi-factor authentication; never hand an individual user broad permissions directly. For workloads, the answer is always a role — its credentials rotate automatically through S T S, so there's no long-lived secret to leak. Whichever identity you land on, scope it to least privilege. And when a principal needs temporary or cross-account access, that's exactly when you reach for S T S AssumeRole.

props.heading: Human or workload — then everything else follows
steps: Is the principal human, or a workload calling APIs on its own?
Human: centralize via IAM Identity Center, or groups + MFA — never a one-off user
Workload: always an IAM role — EC2, Lambda, ECS/EKS, no exceptions
Scope whichever identity you land on to least privilege
Need temporary or cross-account access? Reach for STS AssumeRole

scenes.narration: This is the single most exam-relevant table in the whole chapter, condensed to five rows. Reach for an IAM user only when you have a small number of named humans and Identity Center genuinely isn't in play. Reach for a role for any workload, full stop, or any temporary human access. Resource-based policies matter specifically when the resource type supports one — think S3 or K M S — and you're granting a principal in another account. A permissions boundary sets a ceiling on what a delegated identity's own policies can grant — it never grants anything by itself. And S T S AssumeRole is for temporary, scoped, cross-account or elevated access — not a substitute for a normal same-account identity policy you didn't actually need to complicate.

rows.label: IAM User
cells: A few named humans need direct access and Identity Center isn't in play
The org has many humans across many accounts

rows.label: IAM Role
cells: Any workload needs to call AWS APIs, or anyone needs temporary access
You're tempted to hand out its credentials as a permanent secret

rows.label: Resource-based policy
cells: The resource supports one (S3, KMS) and you're granting another account access
The service doesn't support resource policies at all

rows.label: Permissions boundary
cells: You need a hard ceiling on what a delegated admin's roles can ever grant
You think it grants permissions on its own — it never does

rows.label: STS AssumeRole
cells: Temporary, scoped access to a role in another account (or a higher-privilege one)
You just needed a normal identity policy on an existing identity

scenes.narration: Two commands are worth being able to read on sight, even though you'll rarely type them verbatim. Creating a role attaches a trust policy naming who's allowed to assume it — here, an EC2 instance profile. Calling S T S AssumeRole exchanges a trusted caller's identity for temporary credentials tied to that role, complete with an expiration timestamp — no standing secret involved. Access is gated twice along the way: the target role's trust policy has to name the caller, and the caller's own identity policy has to permit calling AssumeRole on that specific role in the first place. Only once both checks pass does the caller get a session token, and every call made with it is now authorized against the assumed role's own policies, not the original caller's.

props.heading: The real AssumeRole flow, from the command line

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. A financial-services company hires an outside audit firm for a two-week engagement, and the auditors need read-only access to exactly one bucket of financial reports — no console, no other resources. The company doesn't want to create four IAM users it'll never see again, and it wants access to die automatically the moment the engagement ends. Run it through the framework: this is a human, but a temporary, external one, so the answer isn't a user at all. The auditors' own organization has them assume a cross-account role, scoped by its trust policy and an identity policy to just get-object and list-bucket on that single bucket. When the two weeks are up, the company simply deletes the role — there's no standing credential to revoke, because none was ever created.

profile.name: The audit contractor
profile.role: External firm · four auditors · two-week engagement · read-only on one S3 bucket
profile.detail: A financial-services company needs to give an outside audit firm read-only access to a single bucket of financial reports — nothing else — and wants that access to stop working automatically the moment the two-week engagement ends. Creating four throwaway IAM users doesn't appeal to anyone.
profile.verdict: Have the auditors assume a purpose-built cross-account role, scoped by its trust policy and an identity policy to exactly GetObject and ListBucket on that one bucket. When the engagement ends, delete the role — there was never a standing user or key to revoke.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a role's own policy allows get-object, but a separate policy on that same role has an explicit Deny for all S3 actions on that bucket — which one wins? Second, and this one trips up even people who've used AWS for years: a role's permissions boundary limits it to read-only S3, but a bucket's resource-based policy independently grants that same role put-object on one object — does the boundary block that grant too?

questions.prompt: A role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on a bucket. A separate policy on the same role contains an explicit Deny for s3:* on that same bucket. What happens when the role calls GetObject?
options: Denied — the explicit Deny always wins over any Allow
Allowed — the Allow statement was attached first, so it takes precedence
Allowed, but only when MFA was used for the call
It depends on which statement has the lower Sid value

questions.prompt: A role's permissions boundary limits it to read-only S3 actions. Its own identity policy separately grants PutObject, and a bucket's resource-based policy independently grants that same role PutObject on one object. Does the boundary block the resource-policy grant too?
options: Yes — a permissions boundary caps every grant the role can ever receive, from any source
No — the boundary only caps what the role's own identity policies can grant; the resource-based grant stands on its own
It depends on whether the boundary was attached before or after the bucket policy
No — permissions boundaries only apply to IAM users, never to roles

scenes.narration: Here's why. An explicit Deny is checked first and wins outright — the evaluation never even reaches a 'which Allow wins' question, because Deny short-circuits the whole thing. And a permissions boundary only caps what the role's own identity policies can grant — it has zero authority over a resource-based policy attached somewhere else. The role's own attempt at put-object gets capped by the boundary and denied, but the bucket policy's independent grant is evaluated entirely on its own terms. That exact distinction shows up constantly as a professional-level trap.

answers.prompt: Identity policy Allows GetObject; a separate policy on the same role explicitly Denies s3:* on that bucket.
answers.correct: Denied — the explicit Deny always wins over any Allow.
answers.rationale: AWS checks for an applicable explicit Deny first. If one exists, the request is denied regardless of how many Allow statements exist elsewhere — statement order and Sid values don't change that, and MFA presence only matters if a policy's Condition specifically checks for it.

answers.prompt: A read-only permissions boundary vs. a resource-based policy independently granting PutObject.
answers.correct: No — the boundary only caps the role's own identity policies; the resource-based grant is evaluated on its own terms.
answers.rationale: A permissions boundary sets a ceiling on what an identity's own attached policies can grant it. It has no authority over a resource-based policy attached to a completely different resource — that grant stands or falls on its own logic. Mixing this up is one of the most common professional-level trap answers.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. The evaluation order is explicit Deny, then explicit Allow, then implicit deny, and that order never changes. Workload identity is always a role, never a long-lived key — no exceptions the exam expects you to accept. MFA and least privilege are the two most heavily tested security principles on either exam. A permissions boundary caps what an identity's own policies can grant it, but has no say over a resource-based policy granting that same identity access from outside. And S T S AssumeRole is gated twice — by the target role's trust policy and by the caller's own identity policy — both have to agree. Next: chapter three moves from who's allowed to act to where things actually sit on the network — a perfectly scoped IAM policy still won't save a resource that's reachable from anywhere on the internet.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Evaluation order is fixed: explicit Deny, then explicit Allow, then implicit Deny — always in that order.
Workload identity is always a role, never a long-lived key — EC2, Lambda, ECS/EKS, no exceptions.
MFA and least privilege are the two most heavily tested security principles on both exams.
A permissions boundary caps an identity's own policies — it never limits a resource-based policy granting access from outside.
STS AssumeRole is gated twice: the target role's trust policy, and the caller's own identity policy — both must agree.

A retail company's order-processing Lambda function currently reads an old IAM user's access key from an environment variable to write to DynamoDB, and nobody's sure whether that key has ever been rotated. Using this chapter's framework, what should replace it, and what actually changes once you make that switch? There's a specific, correct answer here — not just a vague direction.

props.prompt: A retail company's Lambda function reads a two-year-old IAM user's access key from an environment variable to write to DynamoDB. Using this chapter's framework, what should replace it, and what three things change once you make that switch?
